pattern.title: Reading Comprehension
pattern.description: Passage-based comprehension. Every question needs a passage set.

sets.title: Scan and Pay
sets.text: When a vegetable seller in Madurai pasted a printed QR code on her weighing scale three years ago, her regular customers laughed. Today she says she rarely carries change at all. The Unified Payments Interface has made it possible for a tea stall, a flower vendor and a large supermarket to accept money through the same simple scan, with no card machine and no monthly fee. Supporters call this the most important financial reform of the decade, since it has drawn millions of small traders into the formal banking system. Yet the picture is not wholly bright. Network failures in smaller towns can leave a vendor unpaid for a day's sale, and elderly customers often avoid the system out of fear of fraud. Banks and the regulator have introduced limits, reversal procedures and awareness drives, but these measures work best where people already own a smartphone. The challenge now is less about technology than about reaching those who have been left on the other side of the screen.

sets.title: From Village Ground to Prime Time
sets.text: Until a little over a decade ago, kabaddi was a game played on dusty village grounds and watched by neighbours who had gathered to cheer. The arrival of a franchise league, with floodlights, commentary and prime-time television, changed its fortunes almost overnight. Players who once earned only the praise of their villages now sign contracts worth lakhs, and schoolchildren in cities that had never seen a raid now ask for kabaddi mats. Purists, however, worry that the pursuit of television audiences has altered the sport. Matches have been shortened, rules adjusted to favour dramatic raids, and the loud music between halves would have baffled the old village referees. Yet it is hard to argue with the results: more girls and boys are taking up the sport, and several former rural players have become coaches. The game has gained a larger audience, though whether it has kept its soul is a question its followers answer according to their age.

sets.title: The Return of the Poor Man's Grain
sets.text: Ragi, jowar and bajra were once called poor people's grains, and for a generation of urban Indians they vanished from the dinner table, replaced by polished rice and refined wheat. Nutrition scientists now say that this was a costly mistake. Millets are rich in fibre, minerals and slow-releasing carbohydrates, and they grow with remarkably little water on land where rice would fail. Agricultural departments in several states have therefore begun to buy millets for school meals and public distribution. Farmers, however, need more than official goodwill. Unless markets pay a steady price and processing machines reduce the labour of removing the husk, many will continue to grow the more profitable crops they know. The revival of millets will therefore depend as much on the economics of the farm as on the fashions of the kitchen.

sets.title: Links in a Chain
sets.text: Bengaluru was once a city of more than a thousand lakes, built by farmers and rulers over centuries to store the scarce rain of the Deccan plateau. Each tank was linked to the next, so that overflow from one filled its neighbour and floods were largely kept at bay. As the city expanded, builders drained many of these water bodies and paved over the channels that joined them. The consequence is visible every monsoon, when a heavy shower turns roads into rivers and stranded commuters wait for hours. Civic bodies have started to clean and restore a few lakes, and residents' groups have guarded them vigilantly. But restoring a lake in isolation achieves little if the stream that fed it is still buried under concrete. The old engineers understood that a lake is not an ornament; it is one link in a chain, and the chain is only as good as its weakest link.

sets.title: Chess Beyond the Club
sets.text: When Viswanathan Anand won his first world title, chess in India was largely a pastime for retired clerks and a handful of college clubs. A generation later, teenagers from Chennai and Kolkata routinely defeat grandmasters twice their age, and the country counts dozens of grandmasters of its own. Several factors explain this change. Online platforms allow a child in a small town to play hundreds of games a week against strong opponents. Free analysis engines have replaced expensive coaching for those who cannot afford it. State governments have also begun to reward medal winners with jobs and prize money. Some coaches caution, though, that screens can teach tactics but not temperament; the patience to sit through a six-hour tournament game, they say, still comes only from playing across a real board. Perhaps the best outcome would be a blend of both worlds.

sets.title: Doctor on the Screen
sets.text: A farmer in a Himalayan village, whose nearest hospital is a day's journey away, can now describe his chest pain to a doctor in Chandigarh through a video call at the village health centre. Telemedicine, which was a modest experiment in India for years, grew rapidly when travel became difficult, and many state governments have since built it into their health plans. Doctors report that it works well for follow-up visits, for common ailments and for advice on managing long-term conditions. It cannot, naturally, replace a physical examination in emergencies, and doctors are quick to warn against diagnosis by guesswork over a poor connection. A further hurdle is that the health worker at the village centre often lacks training in handling the equipment. Still, early experience suggests that a good idea, supported by modest investment in training and bandwidth, can bring specialist advice to places that have long done without it.

sets.title: The Kota Dream
sets.text: Every year, thousands of teenagers leave their homes in small towns and move to Kota to prepare for engineering and medical entrance examinations. The city's coaching institutes have built a reputation for producing top ranks, and an economy of hostels, tiffin services and stationery shops depends on the migration. Parents see the fees as an investment, a safe route to a stable career. Counsellors, however, have grown concerned about the pressure borne by students who spend twelve hours a day on tests and are rarely seen to relax. Some institutes have begun to hold weekly fun events and to appoint psychologists, and the state has proposed rules on student wellbeing. These are welcome, but they treat the symptoms. The root of the problem is a system in which a few thousand seats are chased by lakhs of hopefuls, and where a single rank can seem to decide a whole life.

sets.title: Lakes of Bengaluru
sets.text: Bengaluru was once known as a city of a thousand lakes, built by farmers and local chieftains to catch the scant rain and recharge wells. These tanks were linked by channels, so that an overflow from one fed the next, and entire neighbourhoods drew their water from them. As the city grew into a technology hub, many lakes were filled to make way for apartments, bus depots and roads. Today fewer than a hundred survive, and several of those are choked with sewage. Citizen groups have begun to clean a few, removing silt, planting reeds at the edges and fencing off dumping spots. Engineers admit that restoring one lake achieves little unless the channels that connect it are also restored, and these are now buried under buildings. Still, a cleaned lake brings back egrets and kingfishers within a year, which encourages volunteers. The lesson, say the activists, is that a city that forgets how it once stored water will pay dearly when the monsoon fails.

sets.title: The Last Weavers of Pochampally
sets.text: In the lanes of Pochampally, the click of a handloom still begins before sunrise. The ikat technique practised here requires the yarn to be tied and dyed in patterns before it is woven, so that a design appears only when the cloth is on the loom. A single sari can take a family a week or more. Power looms in larger towns now copy these patterns in a day and sell them at half the price, and many young people in weaving families prefer jobs in hotels or call centres. Cooperative societies have responded by finding urban buyers, promoting a geographical indication tag that marks genuine work, and holding workshops for designers who wish to experiment with colour. Some weavers welcome these changes, while others fear that fashion will eventually reduce their craft to a passing trend. One elderly master says he does not mind who wears his cloth, so long as someone still wishes to learn how it is made.

sets.title: Why Trains Run Late in Winter
sets.text: Every December, northern India wakes to a blanket of fog, and railway timetables begin to fall apart. Drivers cannot see signals from a safe distance, so trains must crawl through the very stretches where they would normally move fastest. A delay of an hour on one route soon spreads across the network, because the same rakes and crews are needed for the next journey. The railways have fitted many locomotives with devices that warn a driver of an approaching signal even when it cannot be seen, and this has prevented accidents. Yet the devices only make travel safer; they do not make it faster, and passengers still wait for hours on cold platforms. Some commuters feel the railways should simply cancel trains in the worst weeks and give refunds, which would at least let people plan. Officials respond that cancelling services would strand those who have no alternative, and that a late train is still better than none.

sets.title: Cricket Without a Stadium
sets.text: In many Indian towns, the first cricket ground is not a ground at all but a lane, a terrace or a patch of dry field between houses. Children use a taped tennis ball, a plank for a bat and a wall for stumps, and they invent rules to suit the space: a hit into a neighbour's window is out, and a catch off the electric wire does not count. These rules vary from street to street, and arguments over them are a part of the game. Coaches who select players for academies sometimes say that such play teaches things no net session can, for it forces a young batter to improvise against bowlers of every kind. Others point out that talent born in a lane still needs proper coaching, a good diet and access to turf pitches. India's cricketing strength, in this view, comes from the match of an enormous number of casual players with a thin but improving system that finds the best of them.

sets.title: The Cost of a Free Ride
sets.text: Several state governments now offer free bus travel to women, and the early results are visible at every crowded stop. More women are travelling to markets, hospitals and workplaces, and some bus conductors report that female passengers now outnumber men at peak hours. Supporters say the policy returns a daily saving of a few hundred rupees to families, expands women's access to jobs and makes the city more welcoming. Critics counter that revenue falls, buses become overcrowded and the cost lands on the state treasury, which must pay the transport corporation to make up the difference. An economist who studied the scheme says that the policy may well pay for itself if it helps even a small share of women enter paid work, but that the evidence is yet to be gathered over several years. She adds that no scheme is free; the real question is who pays and what is received in return. Until the numbers are in, both camps have reason for caution.

sets.title: Silence in the Examination Hall
sets.text: For many Indian families, a school board examination is the most anxious event of the year. Parents lower the volume of the television, relatives postpone visits and neighbours ask quietly about the date of the Mathematics paper. Psychologists point out that this collective hush, though well meant, can increase pressure, since a child begins to feel that the whole household's happiness depends on a few marks. Some schools have therefore started to hold sessions in which parents are advised to treat examination months as a normal part of life: to keep regular meals and sleep, to allow short games and to avoid comparing children with cousins. Teachers report that students who study in such relaxed homes tend to score as well as, and often better than, those in tense ones. The change is slow, because a culture of anxiety is not undone by one workshop, but a growing number of families are beginning to realise that calm is not the same as silence.

sets.title: Salt Pans of Kutch
sets.text: Each year, as the monsoon retreats from the Little Rann of Kutch, thousands of families called agariyas walk onto the dry, cracked plain and begin to extract salt from underground brine. They pump the water into shallow pans, rake it as it crystallises and carry the harvest in baskets to the edge of the desert. The work continues through the scorching months, when the white surface reflects sunlight so fiercely that many workers suffer from damaged eyes and cracked feet. Though India is among the largest producers of salt in the world, the people who produce it are among its poorest, for the price they receive from traders is low and unsteady. Welfare groups have begun to supply sunglasses, rubber boots and solar-powered pumps in place of diesel engines, which reduces both costs and smoke. Some families, however, remain in debt to the traders who advance them money before the season starts. Until that cycle is broken, one volunteer observes, the salt will continue to taste sweeter to the buyer than to the maker.

sets.title: The Art of the Monsoon Trek
sets.text: Every July, groups of college students from Pune and Mumbai head into the Sahyadri hills to trek among forts built by Maratha rulers centuries ago. Streams run across the paths, mist hides the next ridge and the grass is slippery, yet the number of trekkers rises each year. Local villagers, who once saw few visitors, now earn from guiding, selling tea and renting rooms. This has also brought problems. Plastic wrappers litter the forts, and an overcrowded weekend can leave a narrow staircase dangerously packed. Forest officials say that some visitors enter restricted areas and light fires, and rescue teams are called out almost every weekend. A few trekking clubs have therefore begun to carry back all the waste they find and to insist that members register with the local authorities before setting out. They argue that a hill belongs both to those who love to climb it and to those who live beneath it, and that love without care soon destroys what it admires.

sets.title: The Auto-Rickshaw Driver's Day
sets.text: By five in the morning, Murugan has washed his auto-rickshaw outside his rented room in Chennai and laid a small garland on the dashboard. His first customers are usually fruit sellers heading to the market, and then come schoolchildren, office staff and, after sunset, tired families with bundles. The fare meter, he says, is a mixed blessing: it protects a passenger from being overcharged but also makes it easy for a rival to compare prices. Rising fuel costs and the arrival of app-based taxis have cut his earnings, but he has joined a driver's union that negotiates for fairer rates. His eldest daughter is studying engineering, and he hopes she will never need to sit behind a steering wheel for twelve hours a day. Yet he does not speak ill of his trade. Over twenty years, he has carried brides, patients and politicians, and every passenger, he says, leaves a small story behind on the seat.

sets.title: Libraries Without Walls
sets.text: In several districts of Kerala, a woman on a bicycle now carries a trunk of books from house to house, collecting the ones that have been read and leaving new ones in their place. The scheme, started by a panchayat to reach those who could not walk to the village library, has more than a thousand borrowers, many of them elderly women who had not held a book for years. Readers say they enjoy not only the stories but the weekly conversation with the person who brings them. Authorities admit the scheme's costs are small, for the librarians are volunteers and the books are donations, yet it has revived reading habits that television had pushed aside. Some critics point out that the collection is mostly in Malayalam and popular fiction, which limits its value for students. Organisers reply that the first aim is to bring people back to reading, and that other tastes will grow once the habit is rebuilt.

sets.title: Cooking Gas and the Kitchen
sets.text: For generations, women in rural India cooked over open fires of wood and dung, breathing smoke that doctors compare to the smoke of dozens of cigarettes a day. A national scheme that offered free connections for liquefied petroleum gas to poor households has brought a cleaner flame into more than eight crore kitchens. Health workers report fewer coughs among children, and women say they save hours that were once spent collecting firewood. Yet the numbers conceal a stubborn fact: many families take only one or two refills a year and go back to wood. The refill costs several hundred rupees, which can be a large sum when income is irregular. Researchers who visited such homes found that women often prefer the gas for quick tea but use wood for the large meals, which require much fuel. Unless the price of refills comes down, or a subsidy is made more regular, the cleaner kitchen may remain only partly achieved.

sets.title: Moving Between Two Languages
sets.text: A child growing up in Hyderabad may speak Telugu with grandparents, Urdu in the neighbourhood, Hindi in films and English at school, switching from one to another without noticing. Linguists regard this as a gift, since children who hear several languages tend to be quicker at shifting attention from one task to another. Some parents, however, worry that so many languages will confuse a child and cause delays in speech, and they therefore speak only English at home. Researchers say such fears are largely mistaken: a child may mix words in early years, but this fades, and the full vocabulary is usually larger than that of a child who knows one language. The real risk, they add, lies elsewhere, in the loss of the home tongue, which can fade when a family stops using it, taking with it songs, proverbs and the link with elders. A language, one researcher says, is not a burden to be carried but a house to be kept in repair.

sets.title: The Metro and the City
sets.text: When the metro first reached the old quarter of Kolkata, many shopkeepers feared that the digging would ruin their business. Instead, travel time between the northern and southern ends of the city fell from over an hour to about twenty minutes, and customers who had once avoided the crowded roads began to arrive in larger numbers. Commuters say they now choose homes by the distance to a station rather than to an office. Urban planners note that each new line also pushes up rents near stations, so that the poor who were meant to benefit most may be forced to move farther out. A few cities have tried to control this by reserving some housing near stations for lower-income families, though the results have been uneven. The metro, in this view, is neither a cure nor a curse. It is a powerful tool whose benefits depend on whom the city chooses to include when it draws the map of the new neighbourhoods.

sets.title: Cities and the Disappearing Sparrow
sets.text: A generation ago, the house sparrow was so common in Indian towns that it was hardly noticed. Today many city children have never seen one. Ornithologists link the decline to several changes: sealed concrete buildings with no gaps where birds could nest, shrinking gardens, fewer insects for chicks and the spread of mobile phone towers whose effect is still debated. Studies of the towers have produced inconsistent results, and some scientists caution against blaming a single cause. Citizen groups in cities such as Chennai and Delhi have begun to put up wooden nest boxes, leave out water and grain, and plant native shrubs. Early counts show a modest return of sparrows to some neighbourhoods. March 20 is observed as World Sparrow Day, and teachers use it to start discussions. A small bird, one volunteer says, is a good measure of a city's health, for when it leaves, other changes usually follow.

sets.title: Haggling in the Bazaar
sets.text: In an Indian bazaar, the first price quoted is rarely meant to be paid. A shopkeeper in Jaipur names a figure, the customer laughs and offers half, and a conversation begins which may involve tea, a family history and mutual praise of each other's cleverness. To a visitor accustomed to fixed prices, this can seem tiring, even unfair. Yet many traders see it as an exchange of respect: a buyer who bargains shows interest in the goods, while a seller who yields shows regard for the customer. Economists add that bargaining lets a shop charge different prices according to what each customer can afford, something a printed price tag cannot do. The practice is declining in malls and online stores, where convenience is prized above conversation. Some shopkeepers lament this, saying that without the bargaining the shop loses its character, and a customer, who is no longer a guest, becomes only a payment.

sets.title: Water Harvesting in Rajasthan
sets.text: In the arid villages of Alwar, a few earthen embankments called johads have changed the landscape. Built by villagers with local labour, each johad holds the monsoon rain behind a low wall and lets it seep slowly into the ground, so that wells upstream stay full long after the rains. Over twenty years, hundreds of such structures have helped revive a river that had dried up, and farmers who once left for cities during the dry season now grow a second crop. Engineers who first doubted the method now study it. What distinguishes the johad is not its technique, which is ancient, but the way it is managed: each village decides how the water is to be shared, and no outsider may impose a rule. Government programmes that have tried to copy the structures without that community control have mostly failed. Water, the villagers say, is easy to store but hard to share, and sharing is what the johad really teaches.

sets.title: The Gift of Boredom
sets.text: Children in Indian cities today have more activity than ever before: coaching on weekdays, music classes on weekends and an unending flow of videos on phones. Child psychologists have started to ask whether, in filling every hour, parents have removed something valuable: boredom. When a child has nothing to do, they explain, the mind begins to make its own entertainment, inventing a game, building a model from scrap or watching an ant for an hour. These are small acts, but they build patience and imagination, the very skills that scheduled activity does not teach. Some parents find this idea hard to accept, since empty time seems wasted time, and they fear that their child will fall behind. Experts do not suggest that all structured activity should be dropped; they recommend a small portion of the day left unplanned. They argue that the child who learns to sit with an empty afternoon will later be better able to sit with a difficult problem.

sets.title: A Wedding Season Economy
sets.text: Between November and February, a typical Indian wedding season sends a ripple through the economy that few other events can match. A single large wedding may employ caterers, florists, tent contractors, musicians, drivers, tailors and jewellers, many of them working on daily wages. Estimates of the sector run to several lakh crore rupees a year, and gold sales rise sharply in the weeks before the muhurat dates. Yet the same lavishness worries social critics, who point out that families often borrow heavily to match what neighbours spend, and carry the debt for years. Some communities have responded with collective weddings, where several couples marry in one ceremony at a modest cost. Others retain large celebrations but pare the guest lists. The hope, one economist suggests, is that a family will begin to measure a wedding by the happiness it brings and not by the number of dishes on the menu.

sets.title: Maps and Memory in Old Delhi
sets.text: The lanes of Old Delhi do not appear on a map in any useful way. They twist, double back and end in courtyards, and yet a rickshaw puller can reach any house without hesitation, because he navigates not by street names but by landmarks: the sweet shop at the corner, the mosque with a green dome, the doorway where a cow usually sleeps. Urban researchers who tried to digitise the area found that satellite maps missed hundreds of shops hidden in narrow passages. They then trained local boys to walk the lanes with phones and record each doorway, and the new map was soon more detailed than any official one. The project's leader says that this is a reminder that a map is a made thing, drawn by those who know the place, not a mirror of it. The boys, for their part, took pride in learning to see their own neighbourhood as a stranger would, and discovered how much they had always known.

sets.title: Trains of the Himalaya
sets.text: The narrow-gauge railway that climbs to Darjeeling from the plains was built in the 1880s to carry tea, and it still does so at a speed that a cyclist could match. Its small steam engines puff through the bazaars, passing so close to shops that a passenger could buy a cup of tea through the window. Modern roads have long been faster, and the railway earns less than it costs, yet it has been given heritage status and is kept running with the help of grants. Local people have mixed feelings about this. Some say the railway brings tourists whose spending supports guest houses and guides; others say the money spent on the toy train could be better used on roads and hospitals in the hills. A guard who has worked on the line for thirty years says he does not argue either way. He only notes that nobody has ever asked to stand on a highway just to watch it pass.

sets.title: Cash and the Kirana
sets.text: The neighbourhood kirana store has survived the arrival of supermarkets and online grocers in a way few experts predicted. Its advantages are simple: it is round the corner, it opens early and closes late, and the owner knows which family needs a small packet of tea until the end of the month. Many shops keep a ledger of credit, which functions as a rough form of lending to families that no bank would serve. Supply companies have noticed this and now offer shopkeepers phone applications to order stock, track sales and receive small loans. Some owners have embraced them; others worry that the large platforms will use the data to open competing outlets. A researcher who studied three hundred stores found that those that combined personal service with simple technology earned more than those that adopted neither. The kirana, she concludes, will not be defeated by the supermarket, but it may be changed by the supplier who decides to become a competitor.

sets.title: A Doctor in the Hills
sets.text: Dr Meena arrived in a mountain village in Uttarakhand twelve years ago with a medical degree and a plan to stay for two years. The nearest hospital was a day's walk, women in labour were carried on cots down steep paths and a simple infection could become fatal before help arrived. She trained local women as health workers to recognise danger signs, and installed a radio link with the district hospital. In the first five years, deaths during childbirth in the area fell sharply, and nearby villages began to send for her. Her colleagues in the city sometimes ask why she gave up a career where she could earn ten times as much. She does not reply with speeches. She says only that the question is a strange one, for a person who is useful in the place where she is needed does not feel that anything has been given up.

sets.title: The Language of Road Signs
sets.text: Anyone who has driven on an Indian highway has seen the signs that say 'Speed thrills but kills' and 'Better late than never'. Such slogans, painted with simple humour, are part of the national landscape, and safety officials say that a witty line is remembered longer than a stern warning. But the larger problem lies elsewhere. In many places, signs are missing, faded or hidden by hoardings, and a driver at night may not see a sharp curve until it is too late. A study of road accidents on a state highway found that more than half had occurred at points where a warning sign was absent or unreadable. Engineers therefore recommend reflective paint, standard symbols that do not depend on language and regular inspection of signs. Slogans may please a driver, they add, but only a clear sign will tell him when to slow down.

sets.title: Monsoon Forecasts and Farmers
sets.text: For decades, Indian farmers read the sky the way their grandparents did: by watching the first cloudbank over the Western Ghats and trusting the village almanac. Today the India Meteorological Department issues forecasts based on satellite images, ocean temperature records and supercomputer models, and its seasonal outlook in April is watched closely by markets as well as farmers. Accuracy has improved, yet a district-level prediction remains hard, because rainfall in a single week can differ sharply between two villages only ten kilometres apart. Critics argue that a headline figure such as 'ninety-six per cent of the long period average' tells a smallholder very little about when to sow. Officials reply that the national figure was never meant to replace local advice, and they point to text-message alerts that now reach millions of farmers in their own languages. Whether these alerts are changing decisions in the field is still being studied; early surveys suggest that farmers trust a forecast more when it comes through a neighbour than through a phone.

sets.title: Threads of a Fading Craft
sets.text: In a weaver's colony near Pochampally, the clatter of the loom starts before sunrise and often continues after dark. A single sari in the traditional ikat style may take a family several days, since the threads must be tied and dyed in patterns before weaving even begins. Power looms can imitate the design in a few hours and sell it at half the price, and many shoppers cannot tell the difference at first glance. The government has tried to help by reserving certain designs for handloom producers and by organising exhibitions in big cities. These steps have helped some weavers, but a young man in the colony shrugged when asked if he would follow his father's trade. His cousin, he said, earns more as a delivery rider. The cloth, it seems, may survive better than the craft that produces it.

sets.title: The Quiet Revolution of Anganwadis
sets.text: Few outsiders notice an anganwadi centre, usually a single room at the edge of a village, yet it is the first point at which many Indian children meet the state. A worker, often a local woman paid a modest honorarium, weighs infants, serves a hot meal, keeps vaccination records and teaches songs and numbers. Surveys credit these centres with helping to reduce stunting, and the mid-day food has quietly kept many girls in the habit of attending school. The workers, however, carry heavy burdens. They are asked to collect census data, register voters and record each household on a mobile application, tasks that leave less time for the children. Training is irregular, and some centres lack even drinking water. Reformers argue that the scheme's success so far rests on the dedication of its workers rather than on the support it receives, and that this cannot continue indefinitely. If it is to grow stronger, they say, the state must pay and equip the worker as it would any other professional.

sets.title: Online Classes and the Village Child
sets.text: When schools closed during the pandemic, lessons moved to phones, and for many children in cities the shift was awkward but bearable. In a village in Odisha, however, a single smartphone in a household had to serve a father who worked in the fields, a mother who ran the home and three children of different ages. Network signals were weak, so lessons were often caught in the evening, when data was cheaper but the child was tired. A teacher in the area began recording short lessons and sharing them through loudspeakers at the temple square, which reached children who had no phones at all. Educators note that such improvisation kept many children from forgetting what they had learnt, but cannot replace the daily presence of a teacher. Several months after schools reopened, tests showed that reading skills among younger pupils had slipped by more than a year. The experience, they say, has shown that technology can extend a school's reach but cannot replace the school itself.

sets.title: A Turn at the Spinning Wheel
sets.text: When Mahatma Gandhi took up the charkha, he did not see it merely as a means to produce cloth. For him, spinning was a daily act that bound the educated to the labouring poor, since a lawyer and a farmer sat before the same wheel. It also taught a quiet kind of self-reliance, for a nation that wove its own clothing would be harder to command from afar. Critics of the time, including some admirers, argued that hand spinning was too slow to compete with mills and that the effort could be used more profitably elsewhere. Gandhi replied that the aim was not the lowest price but the widest participation, because millions of rural households had idle hours and no means of using them. Whatever one thinks of the economics, the sight of leaders sitting at the wheel gave a distant struggle for freedom a visible, everyday form that every household could share.

sets.title: Two Tickets to the Cinema
sets.text: Single-screen cinemas in small Indian towns have been closing for years, replaced by multiplexes in malls that sell popcorn at the price of a meal. In one town in Uttar Pradesh, a theatre that opened in 1962 still shows films for forty rupees a ticket, and its owner, now in his seventies, refuses to sell the building to a developer. He admits that most seats are empty on weekdays, and that the projector, bought second-hand, needs constant repair. On Fridays, however, the hall is full of students and labourers who could not afford a multiplex, and the whistles that greet a hero's entry can be heard in the street. Film historians observe that such halls once did more than screen films: they brought together people of different castes and incomes in a shared darkness. If these theatres vanish, the loss will be measured not only in tickets but in the places where a town used to laugh together.

sets.title: Millets Return to the Plate
sets.text: Until the 1960s, millets such as ragi and kodo were staples across the drylands of southern and central India. The Green Revolution then brought high-yielding rice and wheat with assured prices and subsidised supply through ration shops, and millet fields were quietly turned over to the new crops. Today, nutritionists point out that millets are rich in fibre and minerals, require little water and grow in poor soils. A few state governments now include millets in school meals, and urban cafes have begun to serve millet cookies and dosas. Farmers' groups say, however, that demand from towns does not benefit growers unless the market pays them better than rice, and that the processing of millets, which is laborious, still lacks machinery. A farmer in Karnataka says that his grandmother grew ragi because she had to, while he would grow it because he can earn from it, and that the difference is what the new campaign must bring about.

sets.title: Kolam at the Doorstep
sets.text: Every morning before sunrise, millions of women across Tamil Nadu bend over their thresholds and draw kolams, intricate patterns made of rice flour. The practice looks decorative, but it carries several purposes. Rice flour feeds ants and small birds, so the drawing is an act of daily charity to other creatures. The geometry, built on a grid of dots, is also a mental exercise that grandmothers pass on to granddaughters. In recent years, apartment living and the convenience of printed stickers have led many families to abandon the habit. Some folklorists lament this, but others argue that the tradition is simply changing form: colourful kolam competitions in Chennai during the Margazhi month now draw thousands of entrants, and a few mathematicians have begun studying the patterns for their symmetry. Whether stickers or flour, the underlying idea of beginning the day with a small, careful act of creation seems unlikely to vanish altogether.

sets.title: The Millet Revival
sets.text: For decades, ragi, bajra and jowar were treated as the food of the poor in India, while polished rice and wheat, distributed through the public system, became the aspirational staples. The result was a quiet nutritional cost: millets, rich in fibre, iron and calcium, disappeared from many plates, even as diabetes rates climbed. Then the tide turned. After the government declared a year dedicated to millets, restaurants in Bengaluru began serving ragi dosas and foxtail-millet biryani, and start-ups introduced millet cookies and breakfast mixes. Farmers in dryland districts, who had shifted to water-hungry crops, are returning to millets because the grains need little irrigation. Critics warn, however, that fashionable pricing could put millets beyond the reach of the very communities that once depended on them. If urban demand pushes prices up without raising farmers' share, the revival may enrich retailers more than growers. A genuine revival, therefore, must reach the village kitchen and the field, not just the menu of a cafe.

sets.title: Mumbai's Dabbawalas
sets.text: Every working day, about two thousand men in white caps carry nearly two lakh lunchboxes across Mumbai, collecting them from suburban homes in the morning and returning the empties by evening. The system uses no computers. Each box carries a code of letters, numbers and colours painted on its lid, which tells the next carrier at every railway station where it must go. A box may pass through four or five hands, yet errors are reported to be extremely rare. Management scholars who studied the service were struck by its discipline rather than its technology: carriers are shareholders in their own cooperative, so mistakes cost them directly, and the group has met its deadlines for over a century without formal training in logistics. Some visitors expect the carriers to adopt mobile apps, but the dabbawalas themselves see little reason to change something that works. What they have adopted, quietly, is an online booking facility for customers, which handles requests while leaving the delivery chain untouched.

sets.title: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs
sets.text: When Indian Railways began withdrawing some overnight passenger trains from its schedules to speed up express services, the decision looked sensible on a spreadsheet. The slow trains lost money, blocked tracks and carried few passengers per coach. Yet in the districts they served, the effect was immediate. Vegetable sellers who rode the 4 a.m. local to reach city markets could no longer arrive before the morning rush; students from nearby villages missed the early shift at polytechnics; and daily-wage workers faced a bus fare several times the train ticket. Railway officials point out that buses and shared autos fill the gap, and that faster trains benefit far more people overall. This may be true in total, but averages conceal who bears the cost. A transport policy judged only by the speed of the best train neglects the passengers for whom a slow train was the only affordable option. Efficiency measured in minutes saved should be weighed against the livelihoods it quietly removes.

sets.title: Houseboats and the Backwaters
sets.text: Alappuzha's backwaters draw lakhs of visitors each year, and houseboats have become the symbol of Kerala tourism. Over the last decade, the number of boats has grown from a few hundred to well over a thousand. Owners earn good money in the peak months, and hundreds of cooks, boatmen and guides depend on them. But the canals are not wide, and the weight of motor traffic has begun to show. Waste from some boats flows directly into the water, fish stocks near popular routes have thinned, and fishermen complain that their nets are torn by passing hulls. The Vembanad lake, which receives much of the discharge, has seen a rise in algal growth. The state has responded with a licensing cap and mandatory waste tanks, though enforcement is uneven. Environmentalists argue that a smaller number of better-run boats would earn almost as much while protecting the water, since visitors pay for calm, clean scenery rather than crowded canals. Tourism that destroys the very scenery it sells cannot last.

sets.title: Small-Town Cricket
sets.text: In small towns across India, the path to professional cricket used to run through a single local coach with a bucket of worn balls and an uneven pitch. Talent was noticed by chance, often when a visiting selector happened to see a boy bowl. Today the picture is changing. District associations run trials with video analysis, and academies in towns such as Hubballi and Tirunelveli use bowling machines and fitness tests once confined to metros. The effect is visible in the national sides, which increasingly include players from places that were once cricketing backwaters. Yet the gains are uneven. Academy fees remain high, and a gifted boy whose family cannot afford them may still be overlooked. Scholarships offered by some state bodies help, but they cover only a fraction of those who apply. Until selection depends less on what a family can pay and more on what a player can do, the democratisation of Indian cricket will remain half-finished.

sets.title: Reading the Monsoon Forecast
sets.text: The India Meteorological Department issues its first monsoon forecast in April, and farmers, bankers and policymakers wait for it with equal anxiety. Yet the forecast is a probability, not a promise. A prediction of a 'normal' season means total rainfall between 96 and 104 per cent of the long-period average, but that figure says nothing about distribution. A district may receive its entire quota in two violent weeks, flooding the fields, and then stay dry for a month in the sowing window. For a farmer, such a season is a failure even though the national total is normal. Newer models that combine ocean temperatures, satellite data and local weather stations have improved short-range forecasts, and SMS alerts now reach millions of farmers about when rain is likely in their block. Still, scientists caution that long-range prediction will remain approximate, because the monsoon depends on interactions between the sea and atmosphere that are not fully understood. Users of forecasts, therefore, do well to treat them as guidance and keep contingency plans ready.

sets.title: Ikat at Pochampally
sets.text: In Pochampally, a town in Telangana, weavers tie and dye threads in patterns before they ever reach the loom, a technique called ikat. The pattern is fixed in the yarn, so the weaver must align each thread exactly; a slip of a few millimetres blurs the design. A single saree may take a week or more. Power looms elsewhere now print similar-looking designs on cloth in minutes and sell them at a fraction of the price, and many buyers cannot tell the difference at a glance. The weavers' response has been less to compete on price than to prove authenticity: the town's cloth carries a geographical indication tag, and cooperatives train younger members to market directly through online stores. Several young designers have also begun using ikat in jackets and home furnishing, widening the market beyond sarees. It is an encouraging sign that a craft thought to be fading is being rescued not by sentiment but by thoughtful adaptation.

sets.title: UPI and Everyone Else
sets.text: Within a few years, the Unified Payments Interface changed how Indians pay for tea, vegetables and auto rides. A flower seller in Madurai displays a printed QR code beside her baskets, and customers pay without exchanging change. The system succeeded partly because it was free for most users and worked across banks, so no one was locked into a single provider. But the same convenience raises a quiet worry. Small shopkeepers say that when networks fail in the middle of a rush, they lose sales, since many customers no longer carry cash. Older users, who are not comfortable with smartphones, rely on grandchildren to complete payments, and are therefore less in control of their own money. Banking experts suggest that cash should remain available as a fallback, and that simple voice-based options be designed for the elderly. A payment system truly serves everyone only when it keeps working for those with the weakest connection and the least confidence.

sets.title: The Living Wall of Sundarbans
sets.text: The mangrove forests of the Sundarbans act as a living wall between the Bay of Bengal and the villages behind it. Their tangled roots slow cyclone surges, trap silt and shelter fish nurseries that feed thousands of families. When Cyclone Amphan struck in 2020, villages shielded by dense mangroves suffered far less damage than those where the trees had been cleared for shrimp ponds. Yet clearing continues because shrimp farming pays quickly, while the benefits of mangroves arrive slowly and are shared by everyone. Rising sea levels are also swallowing islands such as Ghoramara, forcing families to move inland. Conservation groups encourage villagers to plant mangrove saplings and offer them paid work for it, an approach that treats local residents as partners rather than offenders. The strategy depends on money, though, and funds are usually the first thing cut when budgets tighten. If planting is abandoned, the sea will be quick to reclaim what the villagers had begun to restore.

sets.title: More Than Quiet Rooms
sets.text: Public libraries in Indian cities have long been dismissed as quiet rooms for retired men to read newspapers. A few are proving otherwise. In Kozhikode, a district library now keeps its doors open until late in the evening and runs weekend clubs where children from nearby slums learn to code on shared computers. A Pune library offers a quiet corner for students who have no space to study at home, and its reading room is filled by six every morning. Librarians report that the number of young members has doubled since such services began. What attracts them is rarely the books alone; it is the feeling of a safe, free place to belong. Some officials still view libraries as a luxury, to be trimmed when money is short. That view mistakes their purpose. A library that opens opportunities for those without them does more for a city than another flyover, and it costs a fraction as much.

sets.title: What the Metro Taught Us
sets.text: When the Delhi Metro opened its first line in 2002, many predicted that Indians would never queue, never keep stations clean and never give up their seats. Two decades later, those predictions look wrong. Commuters line up behind painted markers, security checks are routine, and coaches reserved for women are broadly respected. Planners credit this less to any special civic virtue than to design: clear signs, frequent trains, and fines that are consistently enforced. People behave well when good behaviour is easy and bad behaviour is reliably penalised. The same lesson has been applied in newer systems in Kochi and Lucknow, where stations were planned with wide stairways to reduce crowding at peak hours. Critics note that the Metro serves mainly the middle class and that last-mile connectivity from stations remains poor. These are fair complaints, but they concern the reach of the system, not its demonstration that public behaviour can change when the system around it is well built.

sets.title: Chennai and Chess
sets.text: Chennai has become something of a chess capital in India, and the reason lies partly in its neighbourhoods. In many streets, a boy or girl learns the game from an uncle on the verandah long before joining a formal academy. Coaches in the city started offering group classes in schools and later moved online, so that a talented child in a small town can face strong opponents at home. The state government encouraged this by hosting an international tournament and by funding a few young prodigies. Results followed: several teenagers from the city have earned grandmaster titles, and India's teams have begun to challenge traditional powers. Observers caution, however, that early success invites pressure. Children who begin tournament play at six or seven often burn out by fifteen, and the pursuit of ratings can crowd out schooling. Parents and coaches need to remember that the game's joy is meant to sustain a player, not merely the title.

sets.title: The Village That Runs on the Sun
sets.text: Modhera in Gujarat, famous for its eleventh-century Sun Temple, was declared India's first fully solar-powered village in 2022. Rooftop panels on homes and public buildings, together with a ground-mounted plant, supply electricity during the day, and batteries store the surplus for use after sunset. Households have seen their power bills fall sharply, and some now sell extra power back to the grid. The village's transformation matters less for its scale, which is small, than for what it shows. A community with a tradition of sun worship has become a testing ground for sun-based energy; local people, not outside engineers, operate and maintain the equipment. Larger towns will find it harder, because rooftops are crowded and ownership is divided among many tenants and landlords. Even so, Modhera answers a common objection, that renewable energy is suited only to technical experts. If a farming community can manage it, a housing society in a city may well be able to as well.
