Diabetes in India is caused only by the disappearance of millets.
Millets contain less fibre than polished rice.
Dryland farmers had never grown millets before.

questions.explanation: Rice and wheat were 'distributed through the public system' and became the staples, implying wider access. The passage says millets are rich in fibre, and it never says farmers never grew them or that millets alone cause diabetes.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred about the very low error rate of the dabbawalas? (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)

options.text: It results from formal degrees in logistics held by the carriers.
It is mainly due to GPS tracking fitted to each lunchbox.
It is linked to the carriers bearing the cost of mistakes as part-owners of the cooperative.
It is achieved because customers pay extra for error insurance.

questions.explanation: The passage says carriers are shareholders so 'mistakes cost them directly', and also says there is no computer system or formal logistics training. So ownership-driven care is the supported inference.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred about the measures taken by the state? (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)

options.text: They have caused houseboat owners to lose all their income.
They have made fishermen satisfied with the canals.
They have stopped the growth of houseboats entirely.
They have not fully solved the pollution problem because enforcement is uneven.

questions.explanation: The passage says the licensing cap and waste tanks exist 'though enforcement is uneven', and damage is still described. So the problem persists in part. The other options are unsupported.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that earlier, the discovery of cricketing talent in small towns (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)

options.text: was done through video analysis of every boy.
depended largely on chance.
was handled by well-funded district academies.
was impossible for anyone without a scholarship.

questions.explanation: The passage says that earlier 'talent was noticed by chance', as when a visiting selector happened to watch a boy bowl. Academies and video analysis are described as recent changes.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)

options.text: Floods cannot occur in a season of normal total rainfall.
The April forecast of the IMD is usually wrong.
A forecast of a normal season does not guarantee a good season for every farmer.
SMS alerts have made long-range forecasting exact.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the example of a district getting its quota in two weeks and then going dry in the sowing window, even when the national total is normal. It does not say April forecasts are usually wrong or that floods cannot occur.
questions.shortcut: Look for the example in the passage that the option generalises.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)

options.text: Mangrove clearing continues because it brings quick private profit despite long-term collective risk.
Shrimp farming is banned throughout the Sundarbans.
Mangroves grow best on land cleared for ponds.
Ghoramara is protected by dense mangroves.

questions.explanation: The passage says shrimp farming 'pays quickly' while mangrove benefits 'arrive slowly and are shared by everyone', explaining continued clearing. Nothing supports a ban, and Ghoramara is described as being swallowed by the sea.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that farmers

options.text: no longer need information at the district level
may act on a forecast more readily when someone they know passes it on
have stopped using any kind of weather prediction
are unaffected by satellite-based forecasting in any way

questions.explanation: The last sentence reports that farmers trust a forecast more when it comes through a neighbour. The other options either contradict the passage (they still need local advice) or go beyond it.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that before the franchise league

options.text: girls were not allowed to watch kabaddi
kabaddi was unknown in all Indian villages
there were no referees in kabaddi matches
most kabaddi players earned little money from the sport

questions.explanation: The passage says players once earned only the praise of their villages, which implies little or no money. The other options are not supported.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the severe flooding in modern Bengaluru is largely due to

options.text: more rainfall than in earlier centuries
the loss of the linked system of lakes and channels
the cleaning of a few lakes by civic bodies
the vigilance of residents' groups

questions.explanation: The passage links floods to drained lakes and paved channels. It never claims rainfall has increased.

questions.questionText: The coaches mentioned in the passage would most probably agree that

options.text: children should combine online practice with games on a physical board
online platforms are useless for learning chess
teenagers should not play against grandmasters
tournament games should be shortened below six hours

questions.explanation: Their caution is that screens cannot teach temperament, which real boards do; they do not reject online play.

questions.questionText: The young man's remark about his cousin suggests that

options.text: delivery riding is a respected traditional trade
power looms are banned in the colony
many young people do not see handloom weaving as financially attractive
government exhibitions have failed in every city

questions.explanation: He contrasts weaving with the better earnings of a delivery rider, which points to weak financial appeal for youth.

questions.questionText: The author implies that the wellbeing measures taken by institutes

options.text: have completely solved the problem
are unwelcome
are harmful to students
do not address the basic cause of student stress

questions.explanation: 'Welcome, but they treat the symptoms' shows they help but do not reach the root cause.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that restoring a single lake in isolation

options.text: has already solved the city's water shortage
is more costly than building a new reservoir
is impossible under any circumstance
is unlikely to bring full benefit without reviving the linked channels

questions.explanation: Engineers say restoring one lake achieves little unless the connecting channels are restored too. The passage does not say it is impossible or compare costs.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.text: Young people in weaving families often see other careers as more attractive.
Power looms produce cloth that is of better quality than handloom cloth.
Designers are unwelcome in the weaving cooperatives.
Geographical indication tags have ended all imitation.

questions.explanation: The passage says many youngsters prefer hotel or call-centre jobs. Nothing supports the other claims; the cooperatives actually hold workshops for designers.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that one delay on a route spreads across the network because

options.text: the railways do not publish timetables in winter
passengers refuse to board late trains
trains and crews are reused for later journeys
signals stop working across the region

questions.explanation: The passage says the same rakes and crews are needed for the next journey, so a delay passes on from one run to another.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: “The Quiet Revolution of Anganwadis”)

options.text: The centres do not influence children's school attendance.
The scheme's gains depend heavily on the personal commitment of its workers.
Anganwadi workers are well paid and well equipped.
Mobile applications have improved the quality of teaching at the centres.

questions.explanation: Reformers say success rests on the workers' dedication rather than support. The passage says the pay is modest and that extra tasks cut into teaching time.

questions.questionText: From the passage, it can be inferred that the economist

options.text: opposes all government schemes
is certain that the scheme will fail
considers public transport unnecessary
believes the scheme's value depends on whether it raises women's participation in paid work

questions.explanation: She says it may pay for itself if it helps even a small share of women enter paid work, but evidence is needed.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that comparing a child with cousins is

options.text: discouraged by the psychologists and schools described
a requirement of the board
recommended during examination months
irrelevant to a child's wellbeing

questions.explanation: Parents are advised to avoid comparisons, so the practice is regarded as harmful.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that traders' advances of money

options.text: have been banned by welfare groups
guarantee a fair price to every family
keep some workers bound in debt from season to season
are given only to families with solar pumps

questions.explanation: The passage says some families remain in debt to traders who advance them money, and that this cycle must be broken.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the trekking clubs mentioned

options.text: earn their main income from tea stalls
believe visitors have a duty towards the places they enjoy
are unconcerned about safety
want trekking to be banned during the monsoon

questions.explanation: They carry back waste and insist on registration, showing they think visitors are responsible for care.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the teacher who used the temple loudspeaker

options.text: charged parents for the lessons
could not reach any child
disliked the use of smartphones in lessons
found a way around a lack of phones in the community

questions.explanation: Because many children had no phones, he used a shared loudspeaker, a workaround for the lack of devices.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the organisers

options.text: think only Malayalam books are valuable
intend to stop the scheme soon
believe that interest in reading will broaden once people read regularly
pay their librarians high salaries

questions.explanation: They say the first aim is to restore the reading habit, and other tastes will grow after that.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that many families return to wood because

options.text: refills are expensive relative to irregular incomes
wood gives off less smoke
they dislike tea
gas is unavailable in any form

questions.explanation: The passage says the refill costs several hundred rupees, a large sum when income is irregular.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that a family that speaks only English at home

options.text: has a larger vocabulary in every language
risks the gradual disappearance of the mother tongue among its children
will always raise children who are slow in speech
cannot understand Hindi films

questions.explanation: The passage says the home language can fade when a family stops using it.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that housing near metro stations tends to become

options.text: cheaper because of noise
reserved only for the rich
unavailable to anyone
costlier as stations open

questions.explanation: Planners say new lines push up rents near stations.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that Gandhi valued the charkha primarily for its

options.text: role as an ornament
low cost compared with mills
moral and social significance rather than its price advantage
use in commercial trade abroad

questions.explanation: He stressed participation and bonding, and said the aim was not the lowest price.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that shopkeepers who regret the decline of bargaining

options.text: value the relationship with customers that haggling creates
want malls to be shut down
dislike offering tea
prefer printed price tags

questions.explanation: They say without bargaining a customer is no longer a guest, so they value the personal relationship.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that government copies of johads without community control

options.text: are cheaper than village johads
fail because the social management is as important as the structure
succeed more than village johads
are unaffected by who manages them

questions.explanation: The passage says such programmes have mostly failed, stressing the role of community control.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that experts believe boredom

options.text: is always harmful
is a sign of laziness
should replace all schooling
can lead to creativity and patience

questions.explanation: They say it prompts the mind to make its own entertainment and builds patience and imagination.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that collective weddings

options.text: are held only for wealthy couples
are meant to lower the financial burden on families
increase the guest list
are illegal in most communities

questions.explanation: They are described as marrying several couples at modest cost, a response to the pressure of lavishness.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that the theatre owner continues to run the cinema because

options.text: the multiplex has offered him a job
the government pays for repairs
he values its role for people who cannot afford alternatives and its meaning to the town
he earns large profits every week

questions.explanation: He refuses to sell despite empty weekdays, and the hall serves those who cannot afford multiplexes.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that some owners worry about the supply companies' applications because

options.text: the companies might use the data to compete with them
they have no phones
the applications are too expensive to buy
the applications cannot record sales

questions.explanation: The passage states the worry that platforms may use data to open competing outlets.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the final sentence that Dr Meena

options.text: regrets her decision to remain
finds fulfilment in being useful and does not regard her choice as a sacrifice
plans to move to the city soon
dislikes her colleagues

questions.explanation: She says someone useful where needed does not feel anything has been given up.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred that engineers consider standard symbols preferable to text because

options.text: text is illegal on highways
symbols are funnier
symbols can be understood by drivers regardless of the language they read
symbols are cheaper to paint

questions.explanation: The engineers recommend symbols that do not depend on language.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that millet cultivation declined mainly because

options.text: rice and wheat were backed by assured prices and public supply
millets cannot grow in poor soil
millets are poisonous
people stopped eating cereals

questions.explanation: Subsidised supply and assured prices promoted rice and wheat over millets.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)

options.text: Young weavers have refused to sell online.
Power-loom cloth is of higher quality than ikat.
Ikat can be used only for sarees.
The geographical indication tag helps buyers tell genuine Pochampally cloth from lookalikes.

questions.explanation: The weavers 'prove authenticity' with the tag because many buyers cannot tell cloth apart at a glance. The passage also says ikat is now used for jackets and furnishings and that cooperatives train younger members to sell online.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)

options.text: The government has withdrawn cash from circulation.
UPI charges heavy fees from all users.
Elderly people prefer smartphones to cash.
Reliance on digital payments has made small shops vulnerable to network failures.

questions.explanation: Shopkeepers lose sales when networks fail because customers no longer carry cash, so dependence on digital payment creates vulnerability. The other options are not in the passage; indeed UPI is said to be free for most users.

questions.questionText: It can be inferred from the passage that the early predictions about commuter behaviour (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)

options.text: underestimated the influence of system design.
applied only to Kochi and Lucknow.
were confirmed by later events.
were based on careful studies of Metro users.

questions.explanation: Planners credit good behaviour to design, not to special virtue, and say the predictions 'look wrong'. So the predictions had underrated how much design shapes conduct.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: Chennai and Chess)

options.text: The state government opposed hosting international tournaments.
Online classes have reduced children's interest in chess.
Many Chennai players first learn chess informally at home before any academy training.
All grandmasters from the city eventually burn out.

questions.explanation: The passage describes a child learning from an uncle on the verandah 'long before joining a formal academy'. It does not say online classes reduced interest or that every grandmaster burns out.

questions.questionText: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)

options.text: Batteries are unnecessary in solar systems.
Copying the Modhera model in dense cities will face practical obstacles such as divided ownership.
Households in Modhera now pay more for electricity.
No town can ever adopt solar power.

questions.explanation: The passage says larger towns will find it harder because of crowded rooftops and divided ownership, so obstacles are expected, though 'may well be able' keeps the door open. The other options contradict the text.

questions.questionText: From the guard's last remark one can infer that he believes the railway

options.text: should be replaced by a highway
has a charm that ordinary roads lack
is useless to tourists
is dangerous

questions.explanation: People wish to watch the train pass, unlike a highway, implying its special appeal.

questions.questionText: The word 'smallholder' in the passage most nearly means

options.text: a farmer who owns a small piece of land
a trader who deals in small quantities of grain
a village official who keeps land records
a shopkeeper in a small hamlet

questions.explanation: The sentence is about when to sow, so the 'smallholder' is a cultivator; 'holder' of land, and 'small' in size.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'formal' in 'formal banking system' most nearly means

options.text: polite and ceremonious
complicated and rule-bound
officially regulated and recorded
costly and exclusive

questions.explanation: The contrast is with cash trade that goes unrecorded; a 'formal' system is one that is officially recognised and recorded.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'remarkably' most nearly means

options.text: carelessly
reluctantly
briefly
unusually

questions.explanation: 'Remarkably little water' means an unusually small amount of water.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'kept at bay' most nearly means

options.text: predicted
forgotten
welcomed
held back

questions.explanation: Floods being 'kept at bay' means they were held at a distance, i.e. held back.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'imitate' most nearly means

options.text: copy
destroy
exhibit
improve

questions.explanation: Power looms reproduce the design in a few hours, so they copy it.

questions.questionText: In the phrase 'modest investment' the word 'modest' most nearly means

options.text: humble in manner
shy
limited in size
expensive

questions.explanation: Modest investment in training and bandwidth means a small or limited amount of money.

questions.questionText: The word 'scant' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: unpredictable
meagre
abundant
seasonal

questions.explanation: Farmers built tanks to catch rain that was limited in quantity, so 'scant' means meagre or insufficient.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, the word 'genuine' most nearly means

options.text: colourful
authentic
expensive
fashionable

questions.explanation: A geographical indication tag marks work that is real and original, that is, authentic.

questions.questionText: The word 'stranded' in the form 'strand' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: leave helpless without a means of travel
guide to safety
punish severely
transfer to another city

questions.explanation: Cancelling services would leave people who have no alternative without transport, that is, helpless and stuck.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'honorarium' most nearly means

options.text: a loan from the government
a pension after retirement
a small payment given for services
a certificate of appreciation

questions.explanation: The worker is 'paid a modest honorarium', so it is a token payment rather than a full salary.

questions.questionText: The word 'hush' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: loud celebration
slow progress
sudden argument
enforced quiet

questions.explanation: The household lowers noise and avoids talk, so 'hush' means quietness.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, 'restricted' most nearly means

options.text: very dangerous
limited to certain people or uses
richly decorated
completely unknown

questions.explanation: Forest officials complain that visitors enter areas to which access is limited or not allowed.

questions.questionText: The word 'improvisation' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: a makeshift solution created with available means
a technical failure
a government order
a carefully planned curriculum

questions.explanation: The loudspeaker lessons were a resourceful use of whatever was available, i.e. a makeshift solution.

questions.questionText: The phrase 'conceal' in 'the numbers conceal a stubborn fact' most nearly means

options.text: correct
exaggerate
hide
reveal

questions.explanation: Statistics about connections hide the fact that many families rarely refill.

questions.questionText: The word 'fade' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: become more complicated
spread widely
grow louder
gradually become weaker

questions.explanation: Early mixing of words 'fades' means it lessens over time; the home language may also gradually weaken.

questions.questionText: The word 'idle' in 'idle hours' most nearly means

options.text: busy
wasted in play
stormy
unused

questions.explanation: Rural households had hours in which they did no productive work; they were unused.

questions.questionText: The word 'debated' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: approved
clearly proved
argued over and not settled
hidden

questions.explanation: The passage says studies on towers are inconsistent, so their effect is disputed.

questions.questionText: The word 'seep' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: flow slowly through
freeze
rush out
evaporate rapidly

questions.explanation: Water held behind a wall passes slowly into the ground; seep means to move gradually through a surface.

questions.questionText: The word 'scheduled' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: cancelled
arranged in a fixed plan
expensive
accidental

questions.explanation: Scheduled activity is organised in advance on a timetable.

questions.questionText: The word 'lavishness' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: simplicity
extravagance
carelessness
secrecy

questions.explanation: It refers to spending on a grand scale, i.e. extravagance.

questions.questionText: The word 'whistles' in the context refers to

options.text: a signal from a projector
warnings from the police
a musical instrument
expressions of audience excitement

questions.explanation: The whistles greet a hero's entry, showing enthusiastic reaction.

questions.questionText: The word 'digitise' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: convert into a computer-readable form
destroy
expand physically
sell commercially

questions.explanation: The researchers aimed to record the area in digital maps.

questions.questionText: The word 'ledger' as used in the passage refers to

options.text: a shop's licence
a delivery vehicle
a book of accounts
a loan agreement signed with a bank

questions.explanation: The credit ledger records what families owe.

questions.questionText: The word 'fatal' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: very painful
slow to heal
easily treated
causing death

questions.explanation: A simple infection could be fatal means it could kill.

questions.questionText: The word 'stern' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: strict and serious
brief
amusing
confusing

questions.explanation: A stern warning is the opposite of a witty line.

questions.questionText: The word 'laborious' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: completely mechanised
requiring a great deal of effort
pleasant
very cheap

questions.explanation: Processing lacks machinery, so it needs much manual work.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'struck by' (in 'were struck by its discipline') most nearly means (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)

options.text: irritated by
hit physically by
impressed by
puzzled by

questions.explanation: The scholars studied the service and noted what stood out as its discipline, which is a positive reaction. 'Struck by' here means strongly impressed.

questions.questionText: The word 'conceal' in 'averages conceal who bears the cost' most nearly means (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)

options.text: calculate
hide
improve
reveal

questions.explanation: An average combines everyone's outcomes, so it makes it hard to see who is losing. 'Conceal' means to hide from view.
questions.shortcut: Opposite of 'reveal' - the sentence says averages do not show the burden.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'temperament' most nearly means

options.text: physical strength
knowledge of openings
skill at calculating moves
emotional steadiness and character

questions.explanation: It is paired with 'patience' to sit through long games, so it refers to character and composure, as against 'tactics'.

questions.questionText: The word 'improvise' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: practise repeatedly
copy another player
create a response on the spot
avoid a difficult situation

questions.explanation: Facing bowlers of all kinds forces a batter to invent solutions at the moment, that is, to improvise.

questions.questionText: The word 'crystallises' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: forms solid grains as water evaporates
becomes extremely hot
turns completely transparent
dissolves into the brine

questions.explanation: As brine dries in shallow pans, the salt forms solid crystals.

questions.questionText: The phrase 'a mixed blessing' as used in the passage most nearly means

options.text: a gift from a priest
something with both advantages and disadvantages
an undisguised misfortune
a divine reward

questions.explanation: The meter protects passengers from overcharging but lets rivals compare prices, so it has good and bad sides.

questions.questionText: The phrase 'a powerful tool' in the last lines suggests that the metro is

options.text: a machine that needs repair
entirely harmful
only a symbol of modern life
capable of good or harm depending on how it is used

questions.explanation: The author calls it neither a cure nor a curse, a tool whose results depend on choices.

questions.questionText: In the passage, the word 'lament' (in 'Some folklorists lament this') most nearly means (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)

options.text: express sorrow over
take no notice of
question the origin of
celebrate loudly

questions.explanation: The folklorists are contrasted with those who say the tradition is merely changing, so they regret the abandonment. 'Lament' means to mourn or regret.
questions.shortcut: Contrast word 'but others argue' tells you the first group is unhappy.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, 'aspirational' (staples) means (Passage: The Millet Revival)

options.text: cheap and quickly spoiled
difficult to digest
associated with higher status and desired by many
grown only in cities

questions.explanation: Rice and wheat were set against millets, 'the food of the poor', so they were the foods people wished to move up to. 'Aspirational' means that which people aspire to.
questions.shortcut: Look at the contrast: poor man's food versus the aspirational one.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'democratisation' most nearly means (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)

options.text: growing the commercial value of cricket
making opportunity accessible to people of all backgrounds
introducing elections in cricket bodies
reducing the number of players selected

questions.explanation: The sentence concerns selection depending less on family wealth and more on ability. So the word refers to opening access to all, regardless of means.

questions.questionText: As used in the passage, 'contingency plans' are (Passage: Reading the Monsoon Forecast)

options.text: backup plans for unexpected situations
permanent long-term plans
legal contracts with insurers
plans to invest in banks

questions.explanation: Since forecasts are only guidance, users should have alternatives ready if the season goes differently. That is what a contingency plan is - preparation for events that may happen.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'authenticity' most nearly means (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)

options.text: popularity among buyers
great antiquity
the quality of being genuine
low cost of production

questions.explanation: Weavers are responding to cheap look-alikes by proving that their cloth is the real thing. 'Authenticity' means genuineness.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'fallback' (in 'cash should remain available as a fallback') means (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)

options.text: a penalty for late payment
a type of discount
a final instalment
an alternative to use if the main option fails

questions.explanation: Cash is proposed for when the digital network is down. A fallback is a reserve option for when the main one fails.

questions.questionText: The word 'swallowing' in 'swallowing islands such as Ghoramara' most nearly means (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)

options.text: storing safely
submerging gradually
blocking off
eating

questions.explanation: The islands are lost to rising sea level and families must leave, so the sea is covering them. 'Swallowing' is used figuratively to mean engulfing or submerging.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'trimmed' (in 'to be trimmed when money is short') means (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)

options.text: praised
decorated
expanded
reduced

questions.explanation: When money is scarce, officials cut spending on libraries, so 'trimmed' means cut down or reduced.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'prodigies' means (Passage: Chennai and Chess)

options.text: exceptionally talented young people
coaches in schools
tournament organisers
beginners of average skill

questions.explanation: The state funded a few young 'prodigies' and the following sentence mentions teenagers earning grandmaster titles. A prodigy is a young person with outstanding ability.

questions.questionText: In the passage, 'surplus' means (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)

options.text: the cost of installation
a shortage
the amount left over beyond what is needed
a type of battery

questions.explanation: Batteries store the 'surplus' for use after sunset, so it is electricity produced beyond immediate use. A surplus is an excess.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage's description of lane-cricket rules is best described as

options.text: affectionate and mildly humorous
angry and critical
grim and pessimistic
formal and scientific

questions.explanation: The window and electric-wire rules are described with a light, fond touch.

questions.questionText: The author's concluding stance is best described as

options.text: mocking
deeply pessimistic
balanced and thoughtful
enthusiastic without reservation

questions.explanation: 'Neither a cure nor a curse' signals an even view.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the improvement in monsoon forecasting is best described as

options.text: unreservedly celebratory
balanced, noting both progress and limitations
anxious and alarmed
openly dismissive

questions.explanation: The author says accuracy has improved but district-level prediction remains hard, and presents both critics and officials. That is a balanced stance.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage is best described as

options.text: sarcastic
bitterly critical
indifferent
cautiously optimistic

questions.explanation: The author credits UPI with real achievements but ends by pointing to people left out. This is optimism with caution.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the changes in kabaddi can best be described as

options.text: grieving and nostalgic
even-handed, acknowledging both gains and doubts
scornful of the new format
enthusiastic without any reservation

questions.explanation: The author reports the purists' worries but also says it is hard to argue with the results, and leaves the final question open.

questions.questionText: The overall tone of the passage on city lakes is best described as

options.text: earnest and cautionary
light-hearted and humorous
indifferent and detached
hostile and accusatory

questions.explanation: The author warns seriously and offers a reasoned view, with no humour or personal attack.

questions.questionText: The closing remark, 'Perhaps the best outcome would be a blend of both worlds', shows an attitude that is

options.text: entirely sceptical
mocking
sharply critical
conciliatory and balanced

questions.explanation: The author does not choose one side but suggests combining both, which is conciliatory.

questions.questionText: The tone of the final sentence is best described as

options.text: angry
casual and unconcerned
wistful and mildly pessimistic
gleeful

questions.explanation: 'May survive better than the craft' regrets the possible loss of the human skill, hence wistful and a little pessimistic.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards telemedicine is best described as

options.text: hopeful but realistic
uncritically enthusiastic
completely dismissive
suspicious

questions.explanation: The author praises its uses but names its limits and hurdles.

questions.questionText: The author's tone in the passage is best described as

options.text: admiring
amused
concerned and critical
indifferent

questions.explanation: The author worries about students and criticises the system.

questions.questionText: The author's treatment of the debate between commuters and officials can best be described as

options.text: enthusiastic about cancellations
hostile towards the railways
cynical about passengers
even-handed

questions.explanation: The author reports both the commuters' suggestion and the officials' reply without taking sides.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the anganwadi system is best described as

options.text: entirely uncritical
appreciative but concerned about the neglect of its workers
scornful of the scheme
puzzled and undecided

questions.explanation: The author credits the centres with achievements and points out the burdens and lack of support on workers.

questions.questionText: The tone of the author is best described as

options.text: dismissive
balanced and cautious
enthusiastic
sarcastic

questions.explanation: The author presents both sides and ends by recommending caution until evidence arrives.

questions.questionText: The tone of the last sentence of the passage is

options.text: furious
indifferent
cautionary yet sympathetic
mocking

questions.explanation: It acknowledges love for the hills but warns that without care it destroys them.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the technology-based schooling of the pandemic is best described as

options.text: wholly enthusiastic
scornful
fearful
measured and realistic

questions.explanation: The author acknowledges its value in extending reach but also its limits, concluding that technology cannot replace the school.

questions.questionText: The attitude of Murugan towards his profession is best described as

options.text: realistic yet fond
ashamed
resentful and bitter
careless

questions.explanation: He wants better for his daughter but does not speak ill of his trade and treasures the stories.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage towards the scheme is best described as

options.text: warmly appreciative with a brief note of criticism
sarcastic
deeply sceptical
detached and technical

questions.explanation: The author describes benefits favourably and mentions a limitation without hostility.

questions.questionText: The tone of the researcher's last remark is best described as

options.text: fearful
mocking
reassuring and metaphorical
angry

questions.explanation: Calling a language a house to be kept in repair reassures that it is an asset and encourages care.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the economic criticism of the charkha is best described as

options.text: contemptuous
fair-minded and not dismissive
enthusiastic
fearful

questions.explanation: The author presents the criticism and Gandhi's reply, then says 'whatever one thinks of the economics', neutral and even.

questions.questionText: The tone of the volunteer's remark about the small bird is best described as

options.text: admiring in a purely commercial way
flippant
angry
thoughtful and cautionary

questions.explanation: The remark uses the bird as an indicator and warns that its loss signals other changes.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards bazaar bargaining is best described as

options.text: sarcastic
understanding and mildly nostalgic
completely indifferent
disapproving

questions.explanation: The author explains its logic and notes its decline with some sympathy.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards parents who fear empty time is best described as

options.text: jocular
contemptuous
understanding but gently persuasive
alarmed

questions.explanation: The author acknowledges their fear and then presents experts' reasoning.

questions.questionText: The tone of the economist's closing hope is best described as

options.text: neutral and factual
angrily critical
mocking
gently hopeful

questions.explanation: The word 'hope' and the gentle wording show optimism about changing attitudes.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude to the single-screen theatre is best described as

options.text: sympathetic and wistful
neutral and uninterested
hostile
mocking

questions.explanation: The author highlights its social role and regrets the likelihood of its loss.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage is best described as (Passage: “Maps and Memory in Old Delhi”)

options.text: angry
detached
sarcastic
respectful and appreciative

questions.explanation: The author admires local knowledge and the boys' work.

questions.questionText: The tone of the guard's closing comment is best described as

options.text: bitter
gently humorous and fond
coldly critical
fearful

questions.explanation: He avoids the argument but points out an affectionate truth about the railway's appeal.

questions.questionText: The tone of the author in describing Dr Meena is best described as

options.text: admiring and restrained
sorrowful
mocking
envious

questions.explanation: The account is factual but shows respect for her work.

questions.questionText: The tone in the final sentence is best described as

options.text: furious
puzzled
pointed but measured
wholly humorous

questions.explanation: It gently puts slogans in their place and stresses clear signs.

questions.questionText: The tone of the Karnataka farmer's remark is best described as

options.text: hopeless
practical and hopeful
flippant
resentful

questions.explanation: He contrasts necessity with choice and expresses that earning from millets will make the campaign succeed.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the future of the kolam tradition is best described as (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)

options.text: cautiously optimistic
bitterly nostalgic
deeply alarmed
dismissive

questions.explanation: The author admits decline but cites contests and research, and ends by saying the underlying idea 'seems unlikely to vanish'. That is hopeful but hedged ('seems').

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards the millet revival is best described as (Passage: The Millet Revival)

options.text: sceptical and dismissive
enthusiastic without any reservation
indifferent and detached
approving but cautious

questions.explanation: The author welcomes the revival (farmers return, nutrition) yet warns about pricing and who profits. That mix is approving but cautious.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage towards the dabbawala system is best described as (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)

options.text: resentful
mocking
admiring
apprehensive

questions.explanation: The author stresses no computers, century-long punctuality and rare errors, all of which are praised. The tone is admiring, with no mockery or fear.

questions.questionText: The author's tone in discussing the railway decision is best described as (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)

options.text: detached and indifferent
hostile and sarcastic
wholly approving
critical but measured

questions.explanation: The author grants that officials' claim 'may be true in total' but argues the policy neglects the poor. That is criticism expressed in a reasoned, restrained way.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the present state of houseboat tourism is best described as (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)

options.text: indifferent
concerned and cautionary
celebratory
hostile to tourism of any kind

questions.explanation: The author acknowledges benefits but spends most of the passage on damage and ends with a warning. That is concern, not celebration; and the support for 'better-run boats' shows no opposition to all tourism.

questions.questionText: The author's tone in the closing sentence is best described as (Passage: Ikat at Pochampally)

options.text: alarmist
sorrowful and nostalgic
hopeful and appreciative
cynical

questions.explanation: Calling it 'an encouraging sign' and praising 'thoughtful adaptation' shows approval and hope, not sorrow or alarm.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards UPI is best described as (Passage: UPI and Everyone Else)

options.text: appreciative yet cautious
uncritically enthusiastic
bewildered
hostile

questions.explanation: The author credits UPI's success and also lists practical worries and ends with a demand for inclusiveness. That blend is appreciative yet cautious.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards the conservation effort is best described as (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)

options.text: accusatory towards villagers
concerned yet constructive
humorous
resigned and hopeless

questions.explanation: The author warns about funding and sea-level rise but praises the partnership approach 'rather than offenders'. That is concern with a constructive bent, not hopelessness or blame.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards libraries is best described as (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)

options.text: earnestly supportive
mockingly critical
neutral and unconcerned
regretful and nostalgic

questions.explanation: The author praises the new services and criticises officials who undervalue libraries ('mistakes their purpose'). That is committed support, not neutrality.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage is best described as (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)

options.text: satirical
fearful
analytical and approving
cynical

questions.explanation: The author explains why the Metro works and praises its lessons, while granting that criticisms are fair. That is analytical and approving.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards Modhera's example is best described as (Passage: The Village That Runs on the Sun)

options.text: anxious
disapproving
indifferent
optimistic and encouraging

questions.explanation: The author highlights bill savings and local competence, and ends with a hopeful extension to cities. The tone is optimistic.

questions.questionText: The tone of the elderly master's remark at the end of the passage is best described as

options.text: bitter and resentful
indifferent and careless
boastful and self-satisfied
gracious and quietly worried about the craft's future

questions.explanation: He does not mind who wears the cloth, which is generous, but wants someone to learn the craft, which shows concern for its continuity.

questions.questionText: The tone of the volunteer's closing remark is best described as

options.text: ruefully ironic
cheerfully optimistic
coldly neutral
openly hostile

questions.explanation: He contrasts the salt tasting sweeter to the buyer than to the maker, a wry comment that carries sorrow about unfair earnings.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion? (Passage: “Online Classes and the Village Child”)

options.text: Evening lessons are always better than daytime lessons.
Tests after schools reopened showed reading skills among younger pupils had slipped by more than a year.
Technology can never replace a teacher.
Village children were less intelligent than city children.

questions.explanation: The first is a reported finding of testing. The others are opinions or unsupported claims.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion? (Passage: “Two Tickets to the Cinema”)

options.text: Multiplexes are bad for society.
Such halls were the best thing about small towns.
The theatre opened in 1962 and charges forty rupees a ticket.
The loss will be felt in the places where a town used to laugh together.

questions.explanation: Only the first can be checked against records.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: Rainfall in a week can differ between two villages ten kilometres apart.
The India Meteorological Department issues a seasonal outlook in April.
The headline national figure tells a smallholder very little about when to sow.
Text-message alerts in local languages now reach millions of farmers.

questions.explanation: The first statement is a judgement made by critics. The others can be checked against records or measurements.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion?

options.text: Accepting a UPI payment does not require a card machine.
Technology is a smaller challenge than reaching excluded people.
Fear of fraud among the elderly is unjustified.
UPI is the most important financial reform of the decade.

questions.explanation: Only the first statement can be checked as true or false. The others are judgements.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact according to the passage?

options.text: The changes have damaged the spirit of the game.
Matches have been shortened and some rules adjusted.
Kabaddi has a brighter future than any other rural sport.
Old village referees would have disliked the music.

questions.explanation: Only the first can be checked. The second is a purist's view, the third is speculation and the fourth is not in the passage.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a judgement rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: Several state agricultural departments buy millets for school meals.
Ragi, jowar and bajra are millets.
Millets can grow on land where rice would fail.
Moving away from millets was a costly mistake.

questions.explanation: 'Costly mistake' is an evaluation. The other statements can be checked by agricultural data or records.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a speculation rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: The government reserves certain designs for handloom producers.
The cloth may survive better than the craft that produces it.
Ikat threads are tied and dyed before weaving begins.
Power looms can copy an ikat design in a few hours.

questions.explanation: The first statement predicts the future ('may survive'). The others describe present, checkable matters.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion or prediction rather than a reported fact?

options.text: Doctors report that telemedicine works well for follow-up visits.
A doctor in Chandigarh can consult a villager by video call.
Many state governments have built telemedicine into their health plans.
A good idea like telemedicine will succeed if given modest investment.

questions.explanation: The first is a prediction about success. The rest are reported or observable facts.

questions.questionText: In the passage on coaching institutes, which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion?

options.text: Some institutes now hold weekly fun events for students.
Coaching fees are a safe investment.
A single rank decides a whole life.
The wellbeing measures merely treat symptoms.

questions.explanation: Only the first can be verified by checking institutes. The others are views or exaggerations.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements from the passage is a matter of opinion rather than fact?

options.text: The tanks were linked by channels so that an overflow from one fed the next.
Many lakes were filled to make way for apartments and roads.
A city that forgets how it once stored water will pay dearly when the monsoon fails.
Citizen groups have begun to clean a few lakes.

questions.explanation: The first statement is a prediction and judgement voiced by activists; the rest describe things that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the author's opinion or the opinion of reformers rather than a plain fact?

options.text: Anganwadi workers weigh infants and keep vaccination records.
Workers are asked to register voters.
The state must pay and equip the worker as it would any other professional.
Some centres lack drinking water.

questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses what reformers think should be done; the others are descriptions of present conditions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact?

options.text: Children use a taped tennis ball in lane cricket.
Academies select players through coaches.
The rules of street cricket vary from lane to lane.
Such play teaches things no net session can.

questions.explanation: 'No net session can' is a claim attributed to some coaches and cannot be proved from records; the rest are observable.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion? (Passage: “Cooking Gas and the Kitchen”)

options.text: A national scheme offered free gas connections to poor households.
Wood is a better fuel than gas for every purpose.
A cleaner kitchen will be partly achieved only through a subsidy.
Women should never cook with wood.

questions.explanation: The first is a statement about a scheme that can be checked; the others are judgements or absolutes.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact?

options.text: Commuters are happier than ever.
Travel time between the two ends of the city fell to about twenty minutes.
The poor deserve housing near every station.
The metro is the best thing that has happened to Kolkata.

questions.explanation: Only the first can be checked against timings; others are opinions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a statement of fact rather than opinion?

options.text: Sparrows are the prettiest birds in India.
March 20 is observed as World Sparrow Day.
Gardens should be banned in cities.
A small bird is a good measure of a city's health.

questions.explanation: Only the first is a verifiable statement.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “Water Harvesting in Rajasthan”)

options.text: Johads hold monsoon rain behind a low wall.
Engineers who doubted the method now study it.
Farmers who once left for cities now grow a second crop.
Sharing is what the johad really teaches.

questions.explanation: The first is a reflective judgement of villagers; the others are descriptions or reports.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a matter of opinion? (Passage: “Trains of the Himalaya”)

options.text: The money spent on the toy train could be better used on roads and hospitals.
The railway was built in the 1880s to carry tea.
The railway has been given heritage status.
The railway earns less than it costs.

questions.explanation: The first is a view some people hold; the rest are statements that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a statement of fact rather than of opinion?

options.text: Supermarkets are an unnecessary luxury.
The kirana will never be defeated.
A researcher found that stores combining personal service with simple technology earned more than those that adopted neither.
Online grocers are dishonest.

questions.explanation: Only the first reports a finding of a study that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact stated in the passage, rather than an opinion? (Passage: Mumbai's Dabbawalas)

options.text: The dabbawalas should adopt mobile apps for delivery.
Each lunchbox carries a code of letters, numbers and colours on its lid.
Mumbai's lunchbox delivery is the best logistics system in the world.
Discipline is more admirable than any technology.

questions.explanation: The code on the lid is a physical, checkable detail given in the passage. The other three options express judgements or recommendations that the passage does not establish as facts.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements from the passage is an opinion? (Passage: Slow Trains, Hidden Costs)

options.text: Efficiency measured in minutes saved should be weighed against the livelihoods it quietly removes.
Vegetable sellers rode the 4 a.m. local to reach city markets.
The withdrawn slow trains carried few passengers per coach.
Railway officials say buses and shared autos fill the gap.

questions.explanation: The other three report conditions or statements that can be checked. 'Should be weighed' expresses what the author believes is right, which makes it an opinion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: Houseboats and the Backwaters)

options.text: Fishermen complain that passing hulls tear their nets.
The number of houseboats has grown from a few hundred to well over a thousand.
The state has introduced a licensing cap and mandatory waste tanks.
Tourism that destroys the very scenery it sells cannot last.

questions.explanation: The other statements report numbers, complaints, or official actions. The final one is a general judgement or prediction about sustainability that cannot be verified as a fact.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion expressed in the passage? (Passage: Small-Town Cricket)

options.text: Scholarships from some state bodies cover only a fraction of applicants.
Academies in Hubballi and Tirunelveli use bowling machines.
Until selection depends less on a family's means, democratisation of Indian cricket will remain half-finished.
District associations run trials with video analysis.

questions.explanation: The three other options are reported practices that can be checked. 'Half-finished' is an evaluation of progress and so is a matter of judgement.

options.text: A 'normal' season means rainfall between 96 and 104 per cent of the long-period average.
The IMD issues its first monsoon forecast in April.
Users of forecasts do well to treat them as guidance.
SMS alerts now reach millions of farmers.

questions.explanation: The other statements can be checked against records. 'Do well to treat them as guidance' is advice and so is a judgement.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a forecast rather than an established fact? (Passage: The Living Wall of Sundarbans)

options.text: If planting is abandoned, the sea will reclaim what villagers began to restore.
Rising sea levels are swallowing islands such as Ghoramara.
Villages shielded by dense mangroves suffered less damage in Cyclone Amphan.
Conservation groups offer villagers paid work to plant saplings.

questions.explanation: The other statements describe events or practices that have occurred. The first describes what will happen in a future situation and cannot be verified as fact now.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion expressed in the passage? (Passage: More Than Quiet Rooms)

options.text: The reading room of a Pune library is filled by six every morning.
A library that opens opportunities does more for a city than another flyover.
Librarians report that the number of young members has doubled.
A Kozhikode district library keeps its doors open until late in the evening.

questions.explanation: The other three are reports of practices or figures that can be checked. Comparing a library's worth with a flyover's is a value judgement.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion? (Passage: What the Metro Taught Us)

options.text: The Delhi Metro opened its first line in 2002.
Security checks are routine in the Metro.
Stations in Kochi and Lucknow were planned with wide stairways.
The complaints about limited reach and poor last-mile connectivity are fair.

questions.explanation: The first statement judges whether the complaints are fair, which depends on viewpoint. The other three describe dates, design features and practices that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion? (Passage: Chennai and Chess)

options.text: Coaches began offering group classes in schools.
The state government hosted an international tournament.
The game's joy is meant to sustain a player, not merely the title.
Several teenagers from Chennai have earned grandmaster titles.

questions.explanation: The other statements are events that can be verified. What chess is 'meant' to do for a player is a belief about values, which makes it an opinion.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact?

options.text: State governments reward medal winners with jobs and prize money.
Online platforms let a child play many games every week.
Viswanathan Anand won a world title.
The best outcome would be a blend of online and board play.

questions.explanation: 'Best outcome' is a judgement. The other three are reported facts that can be verified.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a statement of opinion?

options.text: A late train is still better than none.
Northern India experiences fog in December.
Locomotives have been fitted with devices that warn drivers of signals.
Fog reduces the distance from which a driver can see signals.

questions.explanation: 'Better than none' is a value judgement. The rest can be checked against records and observation.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “The Cost of a Free Ride”)

options.text: Several state governments offer free bus travel to women.
No scheme is free; the real question is who pays and what is received in return.
The state pays the transport corporation to make up the difference.
Some conductors report that women outnumber men at peak hours.

questions.explanation: The first is the economist's view of how to judge the scheme. The others are reports of conditions or arrangements.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “Silence in the Examination Hall”)

options.text: Some schools have begun parents' sessions on examination months.
Parents often lower the television volume during board exams.
Calm is not the same as silence.
Teachers report that relaxed students tend to score as well as tense ones.

questions.explanation: The first is a reflective claim rather than a checkable statement; the others describe practices or reports.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a statement of opinion rather than fact?

options.text: Villagers earn from guiding and selling tea.
The number of trekkers rises each year.
Rescue teams are called out almost every weekend.
Love without care soon destroys what it admires.

questions.explanation: The first is a general judgement. The rest report conditions that can be counted or observed.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “The Auto-Rickshaw Driver's Day”)

options.text: Every passenger leaves a small story behind on the seat.
His eldest daughter studies engineering.
Murugan has joined a drivers' union.
Murugan has driven for twenty years.

questions.explanation: The first is a figurative, subjective remark. The others state checkable details.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a matter of opinion?

options.text: The librarians in the scheme are volunteers.
Other tastes will grow once the reading habit is rebuilt.
The books in the scheme are donations.
The scheme has more than a thousand borrowers.

questions.explanation: The first is a prediction offered by organisers; the rest are factual descriptions.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is an opinion?

options.text: Millions of rural households had idle hours.
Gandhi took up the charkha.
Hand spinning was too slow to compete with mills.
Leaders sat at the spinning wheel.

questions.explanation: The first is a claim made by critics that can be disputed; the others are statements of what happened or existed.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion?

options.text: Without bargaining the shop loses its character.
The practice is declining in malls and online stores.
Bargaining lets a shop charge different prices to different customers.
A shopkeeper in Jaipur may name a price that the customer laughs at.

questions.explanation: The first is a lament, a subjective judgement; the others describe practices.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is a matter of opinion?

options.text: Families often borrow heavily for weddings.
A family should measure a wedding by the happiness it brings.
Gold sales rise before the muhurat dates.
A large wedding may employ caterers, florists and musicians.

questions.explanation: The first expresses a view of how to measure; the others describe situations that can be observed.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “Maps and Memory in Old Delhi”)

options.text: Local boys recorded doorways with phones.
Rickshaw pullers use landmarks to find houses.
Satellite maps missed hundreds of shops in narrow passages.
A map is a made thing, not a mirror of the place.

questions.explanation: The first is the leader's interpretation. The other statements are reports.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion? (Passage: “The Language of Road Signs”)

options.text: More than half of the accidents on the studied highway occurred where a warning sign was absent or unreadable.
Reflective paint is ugly.
Witty slogans are the best way to stop accidents.
Drivers on Indian highways are careless.

questions.explanation: The first is a reported finding of a study.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact? (Passage: “Millets Return to the Plate”)

options.text: Millets were staples across drylands until the 1960s.
Some state governments include millets in school meals.
The difference between growing from necessity and growing for income is what the campaign must bring about.
Millets are rich in fibre and minerals.

questions.explanation: The first is a view on the campaign's goal; the others are claims that can be checked.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements is a matter of verifiable fact rather than opinion or prediction? (Passage: Kolam at the Doorstep)

options.text: The kolam tradition is simply changing form rather than dying out.
The habit of starting the day with a small act of creation will not vanish.
Printed stickers are a poorer substitute for hand-drawn patterns.
Kolams are drawn with rice flour, which feeds ants and small birds.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements from the passage is an opinion? (Passage: The Millet Revival)

options.text: Farmers in dryland districts are returning to millets.
A genuine revival must reach the village kitchen and the field, not just the cafe menu.
Restaurants in Bengaluru began serving ragi dosas and foxtail-millet biryani.
Millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium.

questions.explanation: The three other statements report events or properties that can be verified. 'Must reach the village kitchen' states what the author thinks ought to happen, a normative judgement.

An Economist's Biography

questions.explanation: The title should capture the scheme and its two-sided evaluation.

A Chennai Garland Market

The Cycle of Books: Reading Reaches the Doorstep
The Malayalam Novel Today
Television and its Dangers

questions.explanation: The title reflects the mobile library on a bicycle bringing books to homes.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the best title for the passage? (Passage: “A Turn at the Spinning Wheel”)

More Than Cloth: The Meaning of Gandhi's Charkha
How to Build a Textile Mill
A Lawyer's Education

Jaipur's Jewellery Trade
